chapter: Early life and the Whitney Bank
title: Getting a night job at the Whitney Bank during work-or-fight
summary: Dodging work-or-fight, Dawson got on the Whitney Bank night staff through a barbershop tip, arranged to leave for gigs, moved to a day job and worked fifty-two years until pensioned.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: Yeah, well, you'd know him if you saw him. I married him up in New York. Well, how did you get the job with the Whitney Bank?
Uh, wake fight or go to jail. You remember when I came? Yeah. Well, that's what made me go to work at the Whitney.
Yeah, but who did you know there at the bank? Did you know anybody?

I'll tell you how it happened. I was hustling. That time I was a gambler. A lot of ways, that's all I, I didn't do no work or nothing. I'd just catch it what I could. And, uh, running around from district to district. What happened, this colored fellow that worked for the Whitney, he was in a barber shop. Smallwood's barber shop on a rampart near, near, near Gravia. Uh, and, uh, happened, this thing come up by the work fight or go to jail. Well, I was dodging the police, you see, cause I didn't have no job or nothing. And I was just saying, well, I better go around and jump up and get in, smallwood's barber shop and catch a news, old newspaper, something like that. And he said, ah, you readin'. And this fellow come in, worked for the Whitney bank. And he said, well, uh, to get his hair cut. So, while he was talkin' to the barber, uh, I heard him, the barber asked him, uh, about where he worked and he told him. He was, uh, straw boss at the Whitney bank. On the night. So, uh, from that on, I heard him, overheard the conversation. So, I told him, I said, well, uh, do you, uh, you got any opening for anybody over there at the Whitney? He said, yeah. He said, uh, you can get a job over there, if you want to work it. He said, where you worked at? And I told him, I didn't work nowhere, but I was trying to get a job, so. So, he said, well, I'm in the power to put you on, you see, cause I'm straw boss with Si Eagle. Si Eagle was the white man with, was the, was the foreman over there with me. On the night. At the main office. St. Charles and Gravy. So, he said, well, you come over there tomorrow, six o'clock, bring your working clothes, you see. And I'll, I'll, I'll have you put on. But it's gonna be on the night, though. I said, I don't care where so long, I have a job. I was so glad to get it, I didn't know what to do. So, uh, sure enough, I went over there and I got on the night. I put six years on the night at the Whitney with Si Eagle. And from that, uh, I had started to play with Kid Renee then. And, uh, I couldn't, uh, it was time to handicap me all the night playing music, you see. So, they had a chief engineer called Joe. And stuff like

Wolf over there, he was in charge of all the, all the, the building help. And I, I, I said, well now, uh, when, when René had to get a job for that night, I couldn't, I had to work, and I couldn't get off, so I fixed it so that, uh, with Joe Wolf, I could lay off and come back after the dance and stay till in the morning, you know, till daylight in the morning, catch up my job, you know, catch up my work. And he told me that it would be alright. So if I had a job till twelve o'clock at night, I could come back, put my instrument, hide it somewhere, you know, in the back, in the back, until I get off and wait till about seven o'clock in the morning. The Iceman used to bring ice and track up all the place there, you know, in the morning, I'd stay there and catch them, the tracks up from ice, drippings of ice. Well then, uh, I was till in the long run, they had Mr. the, Mr. Bodden had a secretary, he had a few on a second floor, and he, uh, was in charge, he was a superchanneler. So Ms. Alfred, his secretary, took a liking to me, cause I used to go out at night and get her a pot of tea and her, her little lunch for at night, you see. And so I got good with Ms. Alfred, and I told her, uh, that I, uh, made, made her believe that my eyes was getting bad, you know. And then all the marble, all the white marble all around there, and I couldn't see, it was affected by it. So I had to go to the doctor and get my eyes treated and get a pair of glasses. So she said, well, alright, Eddie, I'm gonna talk to Mr. Bodden, and I said, they got putting up a branch, say, uh, Longwood Place branch at Camp McCallio. And you go, and I'm gonna have you fix so you can, you can get that job back there, on a day. And she said, you want a day job? I said, yes ma'am, I said, that's what I want. So she had me transport from the night to the day, cause she liked me. And from that on, I just continued to wait for the Whitney Bank. The bridge come through there, Camp McCallio, they tore the, they tore the, the market place down, they built a brand new branch up on St. Charles and St. Charles and they were at
I was transported right on over there, and I stayed there until I retired.
Well, you had to handle a lot of money, huh?
I handled money, everything, bonds, stocks and bonds and everything.
I remember meeting on the street, thought you'd be carrying all that stuff.
Yeah, fifty-two years I put up with the Whitney.
And they put up with you?
Well, they pensioned me. I didn't lose that number, I pensioned me, I'd get my salary right on.
